blocks.content: This topic covers IAM in full, dedicated depth, the real, broader question of exactly who, and what, can actually access real infrastructure through Terraform.
1. IAM Already Touched On
IAM has already come up briefly, in Terraform with AWS topics ahead and in the Environment Isolation topic's honest limits, this topic covers it directly and fully.
Getting IAM right is genuinely foundational, nearly every other security practice in this module depends on it being handled well from the start.
This topic focuses specifically on IAM as it relates to Terraform itself, both the identity Terraform runs as, and the identities of real people using it.
Understanding this well makes every other topic in this module considerably easier to apply correctly.

blocks.content: 2. Terraform Itself Needs Real Permissions
Terraform itself needs real IAM permissions to actually create, read, update, and destroy infrastructure, it has no inherent access of its own at all.
Whatever identity runs terraform apply, a person's own credentials, or a dedicated role, determines exactly what Terraform is genuinely capable of doing in that specific run.
This is worth internalizing clearly, Terraform is not itself privileged, it operates entirely within whatever real permissions it is actually given.
Everything else in this topic is about deciding, deliberately, what those real permissions should actually be.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548595453-642424689.png

blocks.content: 3. A Dedicated Terraform Role or User
blocks.text: 3. A Dedicated Terraform Role or User

blocks.content: A dedicated IAM role or user, used specifically for Terraform, rather than reused from someone's own, personal credentials, is a genuinely important real practice.
This keeps Terraform's real, actual permissions clearly scoped and auditable, separate from any individual person's broader, personal access.
For CI/CD pipelines, covered in their own module ahead, this dedicated identity is typically an IAM role, assumed temporarily rather than a long-lived user.
This separation also makes revoking Terraform's access, if ever genuinely needed, a clean, isolated action, not tangled up with a real person's own account.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548597202-423687242.png
blocks.alt: A dedicated identity for Terraform, genuinely separate from any one person's own access

blocks.content: ["A dedicated role or user, used specifically for Terraform.","Never reused from any one person's own, personal credentials.","Revoking access becomes a clean, isolated action when genuinely needed."]

Never reused from any one person's own, personal credentials.
Revoking access becomes a clean, isolated action when genuinely needed.

blocks.content: 4. Avoiding Long-Lived Access Keys
Long-lived, static access keys are genuinely risky, if ever leaked, they remain valid indefinitely, unlike a short-lived, temporary credential.
Where a real cloud platform supports it, temporary, role-based credentials, assumed for the duration of a single real apply, are the considerably safer real choice.
This is especially relevant in CI/CD, where a pipeline can assume a role for just the duration of a run, rather than holding a long-lived key in its own secret store.
Where a static key genuinely cannot be avoided, treating it with the same care as any other real secret, covered in the previous topic, is essential.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548598913-423252659.png

5. Real, Scoped Policies Over Broad Ones
blocks.text: 5. Real, Scoped Policies Over Broad Ones

blocks.content: A real, narrowly scoped IAM policy, granting exactly the actions and resources Terraform genuinely needs, is considerably safer than a broad, convenient, wildcard one.
This directly echoes the least-privilege principle, covered in full as its own, dedicated closing topic of this module.
A broad policy is genuinely tempting during initial development, real discipline is applying a scoped one deliberately, even when it takes more upfront real effort.
Starting scoped, and adding real, specific permissions as genuinely needed, is safer than starting broad and attempting to narrow later.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548600817-931725613.png
blocks.alt: Real, narrow scope, deliberately chosen over broad, convenient access

blocks.content: 6. A Real, Concrete Example Policy
A genuinely scoped policy names specific actions, ec2:RunInstances, for instance, rather than the broad ec2:*, and specific resources rather than a bare wildcard.
Building this policy incrementally, adding a real, specific permission only once an actual apply fails because it was genuinely missing, keeps it honestly minimal.
This incremental approach takes real, upfront patience, but produces a policy that genuinely reflects only what is actually used.
Reviewing this policy periodically, covered further in the Least Privilege topic, keeps it honestly current as real infrastructure needs change.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548600817-931725613.png

blocks.content: 7. CI/CD and IAM
Recall the CI/CD Integration module ahead, a pipeline running terraform apply needs its own, real, dedicated IAM identity, exactly the practice already covered earlier in this topic.
Modern CI platforms increasingly support assuming a temporary IAM role directly, without any long-lived key stored in the pipeline's own secret store at all.
This is genuinely the safer, more modern real pattern, worth adopting deliberately rather than defaulting to an older, static-key-based setup.
This connection between IAM and CI/CD is worth remembering directly when that later module is reached.

blocks.content: 8. Reviewing IAM Changes Like Any Other Code
blocks.text: 8. Reviewing IAM Changes Like Any Other Code

blocks.content: A change to an IAM policy is a real, meaningful architectural decision, worth exactly the same code review scrutiny as any other significant configuration change.
This directly echoes the same real review practice already covered for provisioner usage earlier in this course.
An IAM change that widens real access deserves particular, deliberate attention, narrowing access is usually genuinely safer to approve quickly.
Treating IAM changes this seriously is a genuinely worthwhile, real habit for any team managing production infrastructure.

blocks.content: 9. A Real, Common Mistake
Combining a wildcard resource and a wildcard action together, effectively granting unrestricted access, is a real, common, and genuinely dangerous mistake.
This often happens innocently, during early development, when the real, specific permissions needed are not yet fully known.
The honest fix is treating that broad policy as genuinely temporary, and deliberately narrowing it before anything resembling real production use.
A policy this broad is worth flagging immediately in any real code review, exactly the scrutiny covered in the previous section.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784548606629-594319287.png

10. Rotating Credentials
Where static credentials genuinely cannot be avoided, rotating them on a real, regular schedule is a genuine, ongoing security hygiene practice.
This limits the real, practical window during which a leaked, forgotten, or genuinely compromised credential remains actually usable.
Automating this rotation, rather than relying on someone remembering to do it manually, is the more reliable, real practice.
This connects directly back to the rotation practices already covered in the Secret Management topic, IAM credentials deserve exactly the same real care.

blocks.content: 11. A Practical Checklist
Before finalizing any real IAM setup for Terraform, a short, honest checklist genuinely helps confirm it follows the practices covered throughout this topic.
Confirming a dedicated identity, scoped permissions, and, where possible, temporary rather than static credentials covers the large majority of real, practical risk.
This checklist is worth running through for every new real environment or pipeline, not just the first one set up.
Building it into a real, shared setup runbook keeps it consistent across an entire team, not dependent on individual memory.

["Is Terraform using a dedicated identity, not a real person's own credentials?","Are permissions genuinely scoped, not a broad, convenient wildcard?","Are credentials temporary where possible, rotated regularly otherwise?"]

Are permissions genuinely scoped, not a broad, convenient wildcard?
Are credentials temporary where possible, rotated regularly otherwise?

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Terraform itself needs real, dedicated IAM permissions, scoped narrowly, rather than reusing a person's own broad, personal credentials.
Prefer temporary, role-based credentials over long-lived static keys wherever a real cloud platform supports it.
Review IAM policy changes with the same real seriousness as any other meaningful code change, especially anything that widens access.
